items.zh: 又天帝釋有普勝殿，於諸殿中最為殊勝。仍於其處有百樓觀，一一樓觀有百臺閣，一一臺閣有七房室，一一房室有七天女，一一天女有七侍女。
items.en: Further, Śakra, lord of the gods, possesses the Palace of Universal Victory, most excellent of all palaces. Within it stand a hundred towers; each tower has a hundred pavilions; each pavilion has seven chambers; each chamber has seven goddesses; and each goddess has seven attendants of her own.

items.zh: 又彼諸天所有地界，平正如掌，竟無高下。履觸之時，便生安樂，下足之時，陷便至膝，舉足之時，隨足還起。於一切時，自然而有曼陀羅華遍布其上。時有微風吹去萎華，復引新者。
items.en: Further, the very ground these gods stand on is level as the palm of a hand, with no rise or fall anywhere at all. To walk upon it brings ease of itself: the foot sinks in to the knee at every step, and springs back the instant it is lifted. At all times, mandārava blossoms cover the ground of their own accord, and whenever a light breeze carries off the withered ones, it brings fresh blossoms in their place.

items.title: The Heavenly Streets, Gates, Gardens, and Assembly Hall

items.zh: 又彼天宮四面各有大街。其形殊妙，軌式可觀，清淨端嚴，度量齊整。復於四面有四大門，規模宏壯，色相希奇，觀之無厭，實為殊絕。多有異類妙色藥叉常所守護。
items.en: Further, the heavenly palace has, on each of its four sides, a great avenue, its shape supremely fine, its layout a pleasure to behold, clean and dignified, its proportions perfectly regular. Further, on each of the four sides stands a great gate, grand in scale, striking in appearance, never tiresome to look upon, truly exquisite — guarded always by many kinds of beautiful yakṣas.

items.zh: 復於四面有四園苑：一名繢車，二名麁澁，三名和雜，四名喜林。其四園外有四勝地，色相殊妙，形狀可觀，端嚴無比。
items.en: Further, on each of the four sides lies a garden: the first called Chariot-Adorned, the second Rough, the third Mingled, the fourth Forest of Joy. Beyond these four gardens lie four more excellent grounds, supremely fine in appearance, remarkable in form, and unmatched in dignity.

items.zh: 其宮東北隅，有天會處，名曰善法。諸天入中，思惟、稱量、觀察妙義。近此園側，有如意石，其色黃白，形質殊妙，其相可觀，嚴麗無比。
items.en: In the northeast corner of the palace lies the gods' assembly hall, called Sudharma, the Hall of Good Dharma, where the gods gather to reflect upon, weigh, and examine the subtle meaning of the teaching. Near this garden's edge lies the wish-fulfilling stone, yellow-white in colour, exquisite in form and substance, remarkable to behold, unmatched in its splendour.

items.title: Day and Night Without a Sun, and the Danger of Heavenly Pleasure

items.zh: 又彼天身自然光曜。闇相若現，乃知晝去夜分方來。便於天妙五欲遊戲之中，嬾墮睡眠。異類之鳥不復和鳴。由此等相以表晝夜。
items.en: Further, these gods' own bodies shine of themselves. Only when a darkening appears do they know that day has passed and night has come; then, amid their delightful play in the five heavenly pleasures, they grow drowsy and sleep. The various birds cease their singing — it is by signs such as these that day and night are marked.

items.zh: 又彼諸天眾妙五欲甚可愛樂，唯發喜樂。彼諸天眾恒為放逸之所持行。常聞種種歌舞音樂鼓噪之聲，調戲言笑談謔等聲。常見種種可意之色。常齅種種微妙之香，恒甞種種美好之味。恒觸種種天諸婇女最勝之觸。恒為是樂牽引其意，以度其時。
items.en: Further, these gods' wondrous five sensory pleasures are utterly delightful, giving rise only to joy — and these very gods are, because of this, perpetually carried along by heedlessness. They constantly hear every kind of song, dance, music, and clamour, playful banter, laughter, and jesting; constantly see every kind of pleasing form; constantly smell every kind of exquisite fragrance; constantly taste every kind of delicious flavour; constantly feel the supreme touch of the heavenly maidens — and their minds are, at every moment, simply carried along by this pleasure, their time passing by in just this way.

items.title: No Sickness, No Ageing, No Want

items.zh: 又彼諸天多受如是眾妙欲樂，常無疾病，亦無衰老，無飲食等匱乏所作俱生之苦，無如前說於人趣中有餘匱乏之苦。
items.en: Further, these gods, for the most part, enjoy pleasures of just this wondrous kind, and are forever free of sickness, free of ageing, free of the innate suffering of deprivation in food and drink, and free of every other kind of deprivation already described as belonging to the human destiny.

blocks.text: The last reading of fascicle 4 is a tour of Indra's palace on the summit of Mount Sumeru. It is the most lavish description in the treatise so far. Notice where it ends: not with delight, but with the warning that the gods are "perpetually carried along by heedlessness". A shorter day; the commentary closes with a look back over fascicles 1 to 4.

Indra's palace has a hundred towers, each with a hundred pavilions, each with seven chambers, each with seven goddesses, each with seven attendants. Master Cháng Bǎi works out 490,000 attendants, then adds that "'hundred' just means many", so the figure is only approximate. The point is abundance beyond counting.

subs.head: Streets, gates, gardens, and the Hall of Good Dharma

blocks.text: The city has four great streets and gates, four gardens, and level ground "like the palm of a hand", so soft that "the foot sinks in to the knee at every step, and springs back the instant it is lifted", strewn with flowers that a breeze keeps fresh.

In the north-east corner stands the **Hall of Good Dharma** (善法堂, *Sudharmā*), "where the gods gather to reflect upon, weigh, and examine the subtle meaning of the teaching". Even in the heaven of pleasures there is a place for the Dharma, and Master Cháng Bǎi notes that some gods do use it.

subs.head: Day and night without a sun

blocks.text: The gods' bodies shine by themselves. They know night has come only when a darkening appears, when certain flowers close and birds stop singing, and they grow drowsy.

Then the warning. Because every sense is constantly delighted, "these gods are perpetually carried along by **heedlessness**" (放逸, *pramāda*): "their minds are, at every moment, simply carried along by this pleasure".

Master Cháng Bǎi tells a story from Asaṅga's circle. Asaṅga's brother Siṃhabhadra (師子覺) vowed to go to Tuṣita's inner court to attend Maitreya, but enjoyed the outer court so much that he forgot to go. Even a practitioner can be lost in heaven.

subs.head: No sickness, no ageing, no want

blocks.text: The fascicle closes by saying the desire-realm gods are free of sickness, ageing, hunger, and the other human deprivations. After the warning about heedlessness, the effect is ironic: they lack exactly the troubles that, for humans, can prompt renunciation. This is why Buddhist tradition calls the human realm the best place to practise. It has enough suffering to motivate us and enough freedom to act.
Thirty days in, it is worth seeing the shape of what we have read:

items: **Fascicle 1:** a single moment of perception, analysed into self-nature, support, object, accompaniments, and activity; then death and rebirth.
**Fascicle 2:** seeds, the womb, the formation and destruction of the world, and the conditions of human life.
**Fascicle 3:** everything classified: matter, mind, and the unconditioned; six hundred and sixty dharmas.
**Fascicle 4:** the three realms measured, from the hells to the highest heavens, with the conclusion that only the uncontaminated is happiness.

blocks.text: The direction is from the most intimate to the most vast, and the conclusion of fascicle 4 turns it back towards practice. Fascicle 5 continues the three grounds of thought with the remaining aspects of the realms and then turns to cause, condition, and result.

quiz.q: Indra's Palace of Universal Victory has a hundred towers, each with a hundred pavilions, seven chambers each, seven goddesses each, and seven attendants each. According to Master Cháng Bǎi, how many attendants is that?
options: 490,000 — though "hundred" means "many," so it is only approximate
quiz.why: 100 × 100 × 7 × 7 × 7 = 490,000. Master Cháng Bǎi: "'Hundred' just means many; counted as a hundred, there would be 490,000 attendants — but it's only approximate."

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what is the ground of the Thirty-Three like?
options: level as a palm; the foot sinks to the knee and springs back; mandārava blossoms always cover it, a breeze clearing the withered and bringing fresh
quiz.why: "Level as the palm of a hand, with no rise or fall … the foot sinks in to the knee at every step, and springs back the instant it is lifted." Master Cháng Bǎi: the soil is soft, sinking knee-deep and springing back level. Compare §28's knee-deep embers: the same sinking and regrowing — in one place ease, in the other dissolution — the two ends of karma.

quiz.q: What is the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharma) in the northeast corner of the palace for?
options: the gods gather to reflect on, weigh, and examine the subtle meaning of the Dharma
quiz.why: "In the northeast corner of the palace lies the gods' assembly hall, called Sudharma … where the gods gather to reflect upon, weigh, and examine the subtle meaning of the teaching." Master Cháng Bǎi: "The gods gather there to reflect on, weigh, and examine the many subtle principles of the Dharma." B resembles the "Rough" garden, where, he says, weapons are kept. Amid heaven's sensory fullness, this hall is a rare place for reflecting on the Dharma.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, how is day distinguished from night in heaven?
options: the gods' bodies shine of themselves; when darkness appears they know night has come — they grow drowsy, and the birds stop singing
quiz.why: "These gods' own bodies shine of themselves. Only when a darkening appears do they know that day has passed and night has come; … they grow drowsy and sleep. The various birds cease their singing." Master Cháng Bǎi: the sun circles halfway up Sumeru, while the Thirty-Three live on the summit, so there is no sun — their own light marks the day.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, because their five pleasures are so delightful, the gods are perpetually carried along by what?
quiz.why: "These very gods are, because of this, perpetually carried along by heedlessness." The text then lists the five senses' constant delights — "their minds are, at every moment, simply carried along by this pleasure." Master Cháng Bǎi: gods sing, dance, and play heedlessly, "living in heedlessness without realising it."

quiz.q: Master Cháng Bǎi tells of Asaṅga's brother, Siṃhabhadra (師子覺), to show the danger of heavenly heedlessness. What happened?
options: he meant to attend Maitreya in Tuṣita's inner court, but enjoyed the outer court so much that he forgot to go
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Asaṅga had a younger brother named Siṃhabhadra, who meant to go to Tuṣita's inner court to attend Maitreya, but had such a good time in the outer court that he forgot to go." Even a practitioner vowed to Maitreya can be swept away by heavenly pleasure — exactly the text's "their minds are … simply carried along by this pleasure."

quiz.q: Fascicle 4 describes heaven's delights at length, then says the gods are "perpetually carried along by heedlessness." In light of §36, how should these pleasures be understood?
options: still contaminated pleasure that ends in falling; only the uncontaminated realm is ultimate happiness, all else is suffering — and heaven's pleasure easily breeds heedlessness
quiz.why: §36: "This alone, therefore, is ultimate happiness; everything else, it should be understood, is suffering." The five signs of decay in §34 show heavenly pleasure cannot last. Master Cháng Bǎi: the gods "live in heedlessness without realising it," as Siṃhabhadra's story shows. A and C are the very ideas the treatise dismantles — echoing §23's saying, "Better to be Devadatta in hell than born at the peak of existence."
